newsitem.title: USA: FERC's Moler says eager to join U.S. Energy Dept.
newsitem.headline: FERC's Moler says eager to join U.S. Energy Dept.

text.p: President Clinton nominated the head of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission on Thursday to replace Energy Deputy Secretary Charles Curtis.
The nomination of FERC chairwoman Elizabeth Moler was subject to confirmation by the Senate.

"I am honored by the president's announcement and Secretary Pena's confidence in me," Moler said in a statement. "The challenge is enormous, and I am excited about it although it will be hard to leave the commission where I have served very happily and productively for eight and one-half years."

Moler led FERC through years of complicated deregulation iniatives. Last autumn, she was widely rumored to be a front-runner for the top job at the Energy Department and had the support of a variety of industry leaders but lost out to Federico Pena.
Curtis had previously said he planned to resign after seeing Pena through the confirmation process.
"He has a great deal of affection for Moler and is very pleased that she's agreed to serve this administration in that capacity," the Energy spokesman said.
Before Moler joined FERC in 1988, she was senior counsel to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee and worked for Sen. Henry Jackson and Sen. J. Bennett Johnston.
If confirmed as deputy secretary, Moler will serve as chief operating officer for the Energy Department.

"With her expertise and experience with utility issues, she will be a tremendous resource to help determine how our nation faces some of the most fundamental changes in how electricity is delivered to homes, communities and businesses nationwide," said Energy Secretary Pena in a statement.
Industry experts publicly praised the nomination, although some privately expressed surprise that Moler would accept what appeared to be a lateral move.

The Natural Gas Supply Association described Moler as an outstanding leader of FERC who helped the agency develop "judicious, balanced, and far-sighted approaches to complex, frequently highly contentious questions surrounding the nation's move to a more competitive energy sector."
